planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in bright shade; this clumping Veracruz cycad forms a colony of subterranean stems and tolerates brief light frost better than most tropical Zamia species.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered shade under a tree canopy, replicating the humid tropical forest floor of Veracruz where this species naturally occurs; deep shade slows growth while too much direct sun in dry climates can scorch the leaflets. Keep soil evenly moist during the growing season but never waterlogged, since the subterranean caudex is prone to rot in poorly drained ground. Offsets form readily from the base over time, gradually building an attractive multi-stemmed clump rather than a single rosette. This is one of the more critically endangered cycads in cultivation, with only a handful of wild populations remaining, making garden and collection specimens important for the species' conservation.
sources: IUCN/SSC Cycad Specialist Group Red List

planting.note: Plant container specimens in spring in full sun on sharply drained, limestone-derived or gritty soil; this Chiapas native tolerates only brief light frost, so it needs a warmer, more sheltered site than Dioon edule.

directions: Site in full sun on lean, fast-draining, limestone-based soil to mirror the low limestone mounds and sandstone canyon walls of Chiapas and Oaxaca where this Dioon naturally grows. New flushes emerge with a striking silvery-blue sheen that matures to deep green, forming a dense symmetrical crown atop a slowly thickening trunk over decades. It withstands drought once established but has notably less cold tolerance than its northern relatives, so gardeners outside the warmest pockets of zone 9b should treat it as a container specimen that can be moved under cover for hard freezes. Avoid overhead irrigation in winter, which encourages rot during the plant's naturally drier dormant period.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in full sun on sharply drained, rocky or limestone-based soil; this micro-endemic canyon cycad from Oaxaca is extremely drought-tolerant once established but resents winter wet.

directions: Plant in full sun on lean, sharply draining, rocky or limestone-based soil, reflecting the steep canyon walls of the Tomellín Canyon in Oaxaca where this species clings to cliffs alongside columnar cacti and agaves. Stiff, blue-gray fronds form a dense architectural crown and the plant shrugs off long dry spells, needing only sparing irrigation through the summer growing season and almost none in winter. Established plants tolerate brief drops into the mid-20s°F, but the seasonally dry, rocky root run is essential to prevent rot during cooler months. This is a rare species in cultivation and in the wild, known from a very restricted native range, so nursery-propagated material is worth seeking out over wild-collected stock.
sources: IUCN/SSC Cycad Specialist Group Red List

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; this Chinese cycad is unusually fast-growing for the genus but tolerates only light freezes, not hard frost.

directions: Grow in full sun with a little afternoon shade in warmer zones, in gritty, well-drained soil kept lightly moist through the growing season and on the drier side in winter. Unlike the stiff, single-divided fronds typical of the genus, Cycas debaoensis produces astonishing fern-like, doubly divided (bipinnate) leaves that arch out from the crown in a loose, spreading rosette, making it a standout architectural focal point rather than a background plant. It builds a substantial underground caudex relatively quickly for a cycad and can be grown in a large container and overwintered under cover in areas colder than zone 9b. Give it room to spread, since a mature crown of fronds can reach considerably wider than it is tall.
